home.title: See how your money habits add up
home.pitch: Arthik reads your bank or mobile-wallet transactions and gives you a financial health score from {lowest} to {highest}, with every point explained.
home.samples.note: Five invented people, each with six months of everyday transactions. Look at a few and you’ll see that the score measures habits, not income.
home.own.title: Your own transactions
home.own.text: Save a statement from your bank or mobile wallet as a CSV file, and Arthik will work out your score the same way.
home.privacy.lead: Your data stays in your browser.
home.privacy.text: Arthik runs entirely in your browser, so your file is never uploaded, and nothing is saved: refresh the page and it’s gone.
home.method.title: What goes into the score
home.method.note: Five measures of your money habits, each scored out of {highest}. Some count for more than others.
home.method.formulas: The score is worked out with published formulas, not by AI, so every point can be traced back to your own numbers.

band.healthy.explain: On solid ground, with room to absorb a setback.
sample.nusrat.kicker: Sample: Nusrat, university student in Dhaka
sample.nusrat.headline: Getting by, with little left over
sample.nusrat.summary: You live within your means, owe nothing and spend about the same every month, which is a solid base. What holds your score back is how little is left over: you keep {savedShare} of your income, and your emergency savings would cover about {bufferMonths} months of essentials. Eating out and delivery is the biggest of your wants.
sample.tanvir.kicker: Sample: Tanvir, freelance developer in Dhaka
sample.tanvir.headline: Saving well, but with big swings in spending
sample.tanvir.summary: Your pay arrives in dollars and changes from month to month, yet you keep {savedShare} of your income, put the same amount into a Deposit Pension Scheme (DPS) every month and owe nothing. What holds your score back most is uneven spending: buying a PlayStation made August your most expensive month. Wants take {wantsShare} of your spending, and your emergency savings would cover about {bufferMonths} months of essentials.
sample.farhana.kicker: Sample: Farhana, office worker in Dhaka
sample.farhana.headline: More going out than coming in
sample.farhana.summary: You earn nearly {incomeMultiple} times what Nusrat has coming in, yet your score is the lowest of all the sample people. Your loan and credit card payments take {debtShare} of your income, and once they are counted you pay out about {overspendShare} more than you earn. Loans from a relative have covered part of the gap, and you have almost no emergency savings. Your wants are a small share of your spending: what holds you back is how much of your pay goes on rent and debt.
sample.arif.kicker: Sample: Arif, MSc student in the UK
sample.arif.headline: Getting by abroad, with little to fall back on
sample.arif.summary: You live on part-time wages and money from your family, owe nothing and put a little aside every month. Even so, you keep only {savedShare} of your income, and your emergency savings would cover about {bufferMonths} months of essentials: those two are where you have the most to gain. Eating out and delivery is the biggest of your wants.
sample.rahim.kicker: Sample: Rahim, construction worker in Singapore
sample.rahim.headline: Sending money home, and still saving every month
sample.rahim.summary: Every month you send about {sentHomeShare} of your pay home, and your score is still the highest of all the sample people. Your spending hardly changes from month to month, you owe nothing, and you keep {savedShare} of your income. Emergency savings have the most room to grow: yours would cover about {bufferMonths} months of essentials.
sample.note: Summary written with Claude. The score itself comes from the formulas in <link>How the score works</link>.
sample.changed: You’ve changed some categories, so the written summary is hidden: it describes the transactions as they were.

upload.title: Use your own transactions
upload.lead: Save a statement from your bank or mobile wallet as a CSV file, and Arthik will work out your score from it.
upload.privacy.lead: Your file never leaves this browser.
upload.privacy.text: Arthik reads it on this device and saves nothing, so refreshing the page clears it.
upload.file.limit: A CSV file of up to {limit} MB.
upload.file.notCsv: “{name}” isn’t a CSV file. Choose a file whose name ends in .csv.
upload.file.tooBig: “{name}” is {size} MB, and Arthik can read files of up to {limit} MB. Save a shorter period of transactions and try again.
upload.file.unreadable: “{name}” couldn’t be opened. Choose it again.
upload.file.allZero: Every amount in “{name}” is zero, so there’s nothing to score.
upload.savings.label: Emergency savings (optional)
upload.savings.hint: Money you could use in an emergency, such as savings in a bank account or mobile wallet, in {currency}. If you leave it empty, Emergency savings isn’t scored.
upload.savings.invalid: Enter the amount in digits, with a point before any decimals, or leave it empty.
upload.errors.title: Arthik couldn’t read this file
upload.errors.title.some: Arthik couldn’t read all of this file
upload.errors.fix: Fix the file in your spreadsheet and choose it again.
upload.errors.fixOrContinue: Fix the file in your spreadsheet and choose it again, or continue with the rows Arthik could read.
upload.errors.more: {count, plural, one {# more problem isn’t listed.} other {# more problems aren’t listed.}}
upload.errors.continue: Continue with {count, plural, one {# valid row} other {# valid rows}}
upload.error.no_rows: The file has a header row but no transactions under it.
upload.error.too_many_rows: The file has more than {max} rows. Save a shorter period of transactions and try again.
upload.error.month_first_dates: Dates in this file look month first, as in {monthFirst}. Write them day first, as {dayFirst}, or as year, month and day, as {iso}.
upload.error.missing_column: The file has no {column} column. Its first row should name the columns, as in the template.
upload.error.missing_column.amount: The file has no {amount} column, and no {debit} and {credit} columns in its place. Its first row should name the columns, as in the template.
upload.error.duplicate_column: The file has more than one {column} column, so Arthik can’t tell which to read. Keep one of them.
upload.error.duplicate_column.debit: The file has more than one column for money going out ({debit} or {withdrawal}), so Arthik can’t tell which to read. Keep one of them.
upload.error.duplicate_column.credit: The file has more than one column for money coming in ({credit} or {deposit}), so Arthik can’t tell which to read. Keep one of them.
upload.error.direction_column: The “{column}” column says whether money went in or out, so Arthik can’t be sure which way each {amount} went. Make money going out negative in the {amount} column and delete the “{column}” column, or use separate {debit} and {credit} columns.
upload.error.direction_column.unnamed: A column without a name says whether money went in or out, so Arthik can’t be sure which way each {amount} went. Make money going out negative in the {amount} column and delete that column, or use separate {debit} and {credit} columns.
upload.error.bad_date: “{value}” isn’t a date Arthik can read. Write it as {iso}, or day first, as {dayFirst}.
upload.error.bad_amount: “{value}” isn’t an amount Arthik can read. Write it in digits, with a point only before decimals, as in {example}.
upload.error.bad_amount.pair: “{value}” in the {column} column isn’t an amount Arthik can read. Write it in digits without a sign, with a point only before decimals.
upload.error.bad_currency: “{value}” isn’t a currency Arthik knows. Use a code from the Currency menu, or leave the cell empty.
upload.error.bad_category: “{value}” isn’t a category Arthik knows for this row. Leave the cell empty and Arthik will choose one, which you can change.
upload.error.bad_quotes: A quotation mark isn’t closed, so {lines, plural, =0 {this row couldn’t be read} one {this row and the line after it couldn’t be read} other {this row and about # lines after it couldn’t be read}}. Add the missing quotation mark, or remove the stray one.
upload.error.extra_cells: This row has more cells than the header. A comma inside an amount or description usually causes it: put that cell in quotation marks, or remove the commas between thousands.
upload.help.title: What the file needs
upload.help.intro: One row for each transaction, under a first row that names the columns. Cells can be separated by commas or semicolons, and numbers can be written in Bengali digits.
upload.help.date: The day of the transaction, as {iso} or day first, as {dayFirst}. A time after the date is ignored.
upload.help.description: What the payment was, as your statement shows it. Arthik chooses each category from it.
upload.help.amount: Money in as a positive number and money out as a negative one, in digits with a point only before decimals: {moneyIn} or {moneyOut}.
upload.help.debitCredit: In place of {amount}, the file can have a {debit} column for money out and a {credit} column for money in, or {withdrawal} and {deposit}.
upload.help.currency: Optional. A code such as {example}. Without one, Arthik uses the currency chosen in the Currency menu.
upload.help.category: Optional. Without one, Arthik chooses each category, and you can change any of them after you upload.
upload.help.creditCard.title: Paying off a credit card
upload.help.creditCard: A credit card bill payment counts towards your Debt payments. If your file also has the card’s own purchases, give the bill payment the category Own-account transfer, so the same spending isn’t counted twice.
upload.help.accounts: You can put several accounts in one file, such as a bank account and a mobile wallet. Money you move between them should also be an Own-account transfer, which the score leaves out.
upload.help.template.note: It shows the layout, with example transactions to replace with your own.
